---
title: "Randomness and records"
subtitle: "`src/rng.ts` and `src/states.ts`: reproducible runs, and the snapshots they produce"
---

Two small modules make runs reproducible and their results usable: a seeded random number
generator, so that the same seed always gives the same run, and a recorder that keeps the
snapshots and the family tree of the cells and writes them as one JSON file.

## Random numbers

JavaScript's `Math.random` cannot be seeded, so the simulation uses its own generator. *Mulberry32*
is a tiny, fast generator with a 32-bit state: each call advances the state by a constant and
scrambles it with a few multiplications and shifts. Its quality is far beyond what a simulation like
this needs, and it is fully determined by its seed.

```{.typescript file=src/rng.ts}
<<rng-type>>

<<rng-mulberry32>>

<<rng-random-seed>>
```

A generator is just a function that returns numbers in $[0, 1)$, like `Math.random`:

```{.typescript #rng-type}
export type Rng = () => number;
```

```{.typescript #rng-mulberry32}
export function mulberry32(seed: number): Rng {
  let a = seed >>> 0;
  return (): number => {
    a = (a + 0x6D2B79F5) >>> 0;
    let t = a;
    t = Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 15), t | 1);
    t ^= t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), t | 61);
    return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
  };
}
```

When no seed is given, one is drawn from `Math.random`. The simulation reports it in
`params.seed`, and the runner and the viewer print it, so any run can be repeated exactly.

```{.typescript #rng-random-seed}
export function randomSeed(): number {
  return Math.floor(Math.random() * 4294967296);
}
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Same seed, same run

A seed fixes every random choice: the initial cells, friction coefficients, division lengths and
shares, deaths and anchors. The physics engine is deterministic on a given machine, so the same
seed and parameters give a byte-identical states file. That is why the simulation takes care to
draw its random numbers in a fixed order (see [the death check](simulation.qmd#leaving-the-chamber-and-death)).
:::

## Recording states

The recorder writes the format the original model wrote (its `LowRes.json` files), so existing
analysis scripts read the output unchanged:

```json
{"1":[{"x":3.99,"y":166.12,"id":1,"an":0.46,"le":3.7}, ...], "2":[...], ..., "lineage":{"1":0, ...}}
```

- The keys `"1"`, `"2"`, … number the snapshots. Each holds the cells of that snapshot, sorted by
  id.
- `x`, `y` is the cell's centre, `an` its [orientation](model.qmd#orientation) as a fraction of π,
  and `le` its length (distance between the end-cap centres); all are rounded to 2 decimals.
- `lineage`, written last, maps every cell id to its mother's id, with 0 for the initial cells. It
  includes cells that divided or left between two snapshots and so appear in no snapshot.

```{.typescript file=src/states.ts}
<<states-cell-state>>

<<states-round>>

export class StateRecorder {
  <<states-fields>>

  <<states-counts>>

  <<states-add-lineage>>

  <<states-add-snapshot>>

  <<states-to-pieces>>
}
```

A cell's recorded state has exactly the fields of the file format:

```{.typescript #states-cell-state}
export interface CellState {
  x: number;
  y: number;
  id: number;
  an: number;
  le: number;
}
```

Values are rounded to two decimals, the coarse graining of the LowRes format. (This rounding alone
can move a cell's tip by a few hundredths of a unit, which is why overlaps are measured on the live
simulation, not on the recorded files.)

```{.typescript #states-round}
export function round2(v: number): number {
  return Math.round(v * 100) / 100;
}
```

### Keeping memory small

A long run records thousands of snapshots of ~1750 cells each. Kept as JavaScript objects, they
would take much more memory than their text, so each snapshot is turned into its JSON text as soon
as it is taken, and only the text is kept. The lineage is an array indexed by cell id, since
ids are consecutive integers.

```{.typescript #states-fields}
private readonly snapshotParts: string[] = [];
private readonly lineage: number[] = [];
private maxId: number = 0;
```

```{.typescript #states-counts}
public get snapshotCount(): number {
  return this.snapshotParts.length;
}

public get idCount(): number {
  return this.maxId;
}
```

The simulation reports every new cell with its parent:

```{.typescript #states-add-lineage}
public addLineage(childId: number, parentId: number): void {
  this.lineage[childId] = parentId;
  if (childId > this.maxId) { this.maxId = childId; }
}
```

`addSnapshot` sorts the cells by id, rounds their values and stores the snapshot's JSON entry,
`"n":[...]`:

```{.typescript #states-add-snapshot}
public addSnapshot(cells: CellState[]): void {
  const sorted = cells.slice().sort((a, b) => a.id - b.id);
  const text = sorted.map((c) => JSON.stringify({
    x: round2(c.x),
    y: round2(c.y),
    id: c.id,
    an: round2(c.an),
    le: round2(c.le),
  })).join(",");
  this.snapshotParts.push(`"${this.snapshotParts.length + 1}":[${text}]`);
}
```

### Writing the file

The complete file of a long run is about 190 MB. Joining it into one string would need that much
memory again at the moment of saving, close to the longest string a JavaScript engine allows. So
the recorder never builds it as one string: `toPieces` returns the file as a list of pieces, in
order. The runner writes them to disk one by one, and the browser passes them to a `Blob`, which
stores them without building a JavaScript string. The lineage is split into pieces of 10 000
entries for the same reason.

```{.typescript #states-to-pieces}
public toPieces(): string[] {
  const pieces: string[] = ["{"];
  this.snapshotParts.forEach((part, i) => {
    if (i > 0) { pieces.push(","); }
    pieces.push(part);
  });
  if (this.snapshotParts.length > 0) { pieces.push(","); }
  pieces.push(`"lineage":{`);
  const CHUNK = 10000;
  for (let start = 1; start <= this.maxId; start += CHUNK) {
    const entries: string[] = [];
    for (let id = start; id < start + CHUNK && id <= this.maxId; id++) {
      entries.push(`"${id}":${this.lineage[id]}`);
    }
    pieces.push((start > 1 ? "," : "") + entries.join(","));
  }
  pieces.push("}}");
  return pieces;
}
```
